AI Community Beyond Bigger Context Windows: 10 Context Engineering Patterns Every LLM Engineer Should Know https://pub.towardsai.net/beyond-bigger-context-windows-10-context-engineering-patterns-every-llm-engineer-should-know-161a75e5f146?source=rss----98111c9905da---4 <p>Large context windows are impressive, but they haven’t eliminated the need for context engineering. In production AI systems, deciding <strong>what not to send</strong> to the model is often more i beyond bigger context windows: 10 context engineering patterns every llm engineer should know <p>large context windows are impressive, but they haven’t eliminated the need for context engineering. in production ai systems, deciding <strong>what not to send</strong> to the model is often more important than increasing the number of tokens it can process.</p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*ebtuq45pw0ljfnr-9tfmug.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 1: context optimization is a loop: retrieve, compress, rank, and assemble only the useful evidence.</strong></figcaption></figure><h3>introduction</h3><p>when frontier models began offering very large context windows, many people predicted that retrieval-augmented generation would become less important. if a model can read an entire codebase, documentation library, or book in one prompt, why bother with retrieval?<br />in practice, the opposite happened. teams building production ai systems still spend significant engineering effort deciding which information reaches the model. larger context windows increase capacity, but they do not automatically improve reasoning, reduce latency, or lower cost. <br />the problem has shifted <br />from : <strong>how do we fit information into the prompt?</strong> <br />to: <strong>what information actually deserves the model’s attention?<br /></strong> this discipline is increasingly called context engineering.</p><h4><strong>why bigger context windows are not enough</strong></h4><p>consider a technical assistant helping engineers troubleshoot industrial equipment. the available information might include manuals, maintenance logs, sensor histories, support tickets, internal engineering documents, and regulatory standards. even if an llm could technically process all of it, that does not mean it should. in practice, indiscriminate ingestion introduces several real operational penalties:</p><ul><li><strong>higher inference cost</strong></li><li><strong>increased latency</strong></li><li><strong>more irrelevant information competing for attention</strong></li><li><strong>greater risk of conflicting or stale information</strong></li><li><strong>reduced reasoning efficiency</strong></li><li><strong>every additional token consumes computation</strong></li></ul><p>every additional token consumes computation. more importantly, every irrelevant token competes for the model’s attention. good context engineering is therefore not about maximizing context. it is about maximizing signal while minimizing noise.</p><h4><strong>context engineering as an optimization problem</strong></h4><blockquote><strong>useful context = relevant information — noise — redundancy + structure</strong></blockquote><p>the objective is not to provide the model with everything you know. the objective is to provide exactly what it needs to solve the current task. this design philosophy underpins modern rag systems, long-running assistants, and agentic ai architectures.</p><p><strong>pattern 1: semantic chunking</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*qlcuovik87ielyrhatbzyw.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 2: semantic chunking preserves meaning by splitting documents at natural boundaries.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>many rag systems split documents into fixed-size chunks, such as 500 or 1,000 tokens. although simple, this can separate related ideas or merge unrelated topics. <br />a better strategy is semantic chunking: split by headings, sections, paragraphs, functions, api definitions or code blocks. <br />each chunk should represent a complete concept rather than an arbitrary number of tokens. this improves retrieval quality because embeddings represent coherent ideas instead of fragmented text.</p><p><em>the following is simplified pseudocode showing the chunking:</em></p><pre>from langchain.text_splitter import recursivecharactertextsplitter<br /><br />splitter = recursivecharactertextsplitter(<br /> chunk_size=500,<br /> chunk_overlap=100,<br /> separators=[&quot;\n## &quot;, &quot;\n### &quot;, &quot;\n\n&quot;, &quot;.&quot;]<br />)<br />chunks = splitter.split_text(document)</pre><p><strong>pattern 2: hierarchical retrieval</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*ngqrqe_2wozhxc4cepcz6g.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 3: hierarchical retrieval narrows search from corpus to document, section, and paragraph.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>instead of searching every paragraph individually, production systems often retrieve information in multiple stages. <br />a system may first identify relevant documents, then relevant sections, and finally the paragraphs most useful for the current question. <br />this reduces search complexity while improving retrieval precision, especially in large enterprise knowledge bases.</p><p><em>the following is simplified pseudocode showing the retrieval flow:</em></p><pre>docs = retrieve_documents(query, top_k=20)<br /><br />sections = retrieve_sections(<br /> query,<br /> documents=docs,<br /> top_k=5<br />)<br /><br />paragraphs = retrieve_paragraphs(<br /> query,<br /> sections=sections,<br /> top_k=8<br />)<br />answer = llm(paragraphs)</pre><p><strong>pattern 3: context compression</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*bkjwnnxef6thhxhaoz0hca.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 4: compression converts long retrieved passages into short task-specific evidence.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>retrieval often returns more information than necessary. an intermediate compression step extracts only what matters for the current query. compression can include key sentence extraction, bullet-point summaries, table generation, equation extraction or code snippet isolation. the model receives the essential evidence without unnecessary detail.</p><pre>from langchain_openai import chatopenai<br />from langchain.retrievers.document_compressors import llmchainextractor<br /><br /># initialize the llm<br /><br />llm = chatopenai(model=&quot;gpt-4.1&quot;)<br /># create the compressor<br />compressor = llmchainextractor.from_llm(llm)<br /><br /># compress retrieved documents based on the user query<br />compressed_docs = compressor.compress_documents(<br /> documents=retrieved_docs,<br /> query=user_query<br />)<br /><br /># generate the final response<br />response = llm.invoke(<br /> f&quot;&quot;&quot; context: {compressed_docs} question: {user_query} &quot;&quot;&quot; )</pre><p><strong>pattern 4: sliding conversation memory</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*jnsijfkog7tp-bhh6sccsq.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 5: sliding memory keeps recent turns verbatim and summarizes older history.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>long-running assistants cannot retain every previous message indefinitely. a practical approach is to keep the last few turns unchanged while summarizing older discussion into goals, constraints, decisions and unresolved questions. this maintains continuity while keeping prompts compact.</p><pre>from langchain_openai import chatopenai<br />from langchain.memory import conversationsummarybuffermemory<br /><br />llm = chatopenai(model=&quot;gpt-4.1&quot;)<br /><br />memory = conversationsummarybuffermemory(<br /> llm=llm,<br /> max_token_limit=1000<br />)<br /><br /># save each interaction<br />memory.save_context(<br /> {&quot;input&quot;: user_query},<br /> {&quot;output&quot;: assistant_response}<br />)<br /><br /># returns:<br /># • summary of older messages<br /># • most recent conversation turns<br />context = memory.load_memory_variables({})[&quot;history&quot;]<br /><br />response = llm.invoke(<br /> f&quot;&quot;&quot; context: {context} user: {user_query} &quot;&quot;&quot;<br />)</pre><p><strong>pattern 5: query expansion and metadata filtering</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*xkm8jqwqwc25l4fsxf0wpw.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 6: query expansion improves recall, while metadata filtering narrows the search space.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>users rarely phrase questions using exactly the same terminology found in documentation. for example, battery degradation may need to expand into capacity fade, cycle aging, calendar aging, state of health and lithium-ion aging. <br />metadata filtering then narrows the search by project, product version, department, author, date, language or security level.</p><pre>from langchain_openai import chatopenai<br /><br />llm = chatopenai(model=&quot;gpt-4.1&quot;)<br /><br /># step 1: expand the user query<br />expanded_queries = llm.invoke(<br /> f&quot;&quot;&quot;<br /> generate 3 alternative search queries for this user question.<br /> keep them short and technical. question: {user_query}&quot;&quot;&quot;<br />).content.split(&quot;\n&quot;)<br /><br /># step 2: search only inside the relevant metadata scope<br />all_results = []<br /><br />for query in expanded_queries:<br /> results = vector_db.similarity_search(<br /> query=query,<br /> k=5,<br /> filter={<br /> &quot;department&quot;: &quot;battery&quot;,<br /> &quot;document_type&quot;: &quot;technical_report&quot;,<br /> &quot;year&quot;: 2025<br /> }<br /> )<br /> all_results.extend(results)<br /><br /># step 3: pass filtered, expanded results to the llm<br />context = &quot;\n\n&quot;.join(doc.page_content for doc in all_results)<br /><br />response = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; context: {context} question: {user_query} &quot;&quot;&quot;)</pre><p><strong>pattern 6: retrieval re-ranking</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*ujaydcenfh3qv5r2znycwq.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 7: re-ranking turns broad candidate retrieval into high-precision context selection.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>vector search is fast, but embedding similarity is not always the same as task relevance. modern systems often retrieve a larger candidate set using embeddings, then apply a cross-encoder or llm-based re-ranker. <br />this often improves answer quality more than simply increasing the number of retrieved chunks.</p><p><em>the following is simplified pseudocode showing the retrieval re-ranking:</em></p><pre>docs = vector_db.search(query, top_k=20)<br /><br />ranked = reranker.rank(query, docs)<br /><br />context = ranked[:5]</pre><p><strong>pattern 7: structured agent memory</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*oiwdskzxgcbwetyjvxqnaa.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 8: structured memory stores agent state as fields instead of raw chat history.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>agentic systems often fail because they repeatedly rediscover information or carry too much irrelevant history. <br />instead of storing raw conversation logs, maintain compact structured state: goal, constraints, completed work, intermediate results and next action.<br />this is smaller, easier to inspect, and better aligned with multi-step reasoning.</p><pre>from dataclasses import dataclass, field<br />from typing import list<br /><br /><br />@dataclass<br />class agentmemory:<br /> goal: str<br /> constraints: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)<br /> completed_tasks: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)<br /> intermediate_results: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)<br /> next_action: str = &quot;&quot;<br /><br /><br />memory = agentmemory(<br /> goal=&quot;write a medium article on context engineering&quot;,<br /> constraints=[<br /> &quot;keep examples practical&quot;,<br /> &quot;use simple architecture diagrams&quot;,<br /> &quot;avoid overly academic language&quot;<br /> ]<br />)<br /><br /># agent completes a step<br />memory.completed_tasks.append(&quot;drafted introduction&quot;)<br />memory.intermediate_results.append(<br /> &quot;main thesis: bigger context windows do not remove the need for context engineering.&quot;<br />)<br />memory.next_action = &quot;write the section on structured agent memory&quot;<br /><br /># build compact context for the next llm call<br />prompt = f&quot;&quot;&quot; agent state: goal: {memory.goal} <br /> constraints: {memory.constraints} <br /> completed tasks: {memory.completed_tasks}<br /> intermediate results: {memory.intermediate_results}<br /> next action: {memory.next_action} &quot;&quot;&quot;<br /><br />response = llm.invoke(prompt)</pre><p><strong>pattern 8: dynamic prompt assembly</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*wbxzsiqvaq1ktuovqliihw.png" /><figcaption><strong>figure 9: dynamic prompt assembly adds only the modules needed for the current task.</strong></figcaption></figure><p>a production system should not rely on one massive static prompt. <br />instead, prompts are assembled from modules: system instructions, user query, retrieved documents, tool outputs, user preferences, examples and agent memory.<br />we include each module only when it applies, which keeps the prompt lean and the system easier to maintain.</p><pre>def build_prompt(<br /> user_query,<br /> retrieved_docs=none,<br /> tool_outputs=none,<br /> user_preferences=none,<br /> examples=none,<br /> agent_memory=none<br />):<br /> prompt_parts = []<br /><br /> # always included<br /> prompt_parts.append(&quot;&quot;&quot; you are a helpful ai assistant.<br /> answer clearly and use only reliable information. &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> # optional modules<br /> if user_preferences:<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; user preferences: {user_preferences} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> if agent_memory:<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; agent memory: {agent_memory} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> if retrieved_docs:<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; retrieved documents: {retrieved_docs} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> if tool_outputs:<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; tool outputs: {tool_outputs} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> if examples:<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; examples: {examples} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> # current task<br /> prompt_parts.append(f&quot;&quot;&quot; user query: {user_query} &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /><br /> return &quot;\n&quot;.join(prompt_parts)<br /><br /><br />prompt = build_prompt(<br /> user_query=&quot;explain context compression&quot;,<br /> retrieved_docs=retrieved_context,<br /> user_preferences=&quot;prefer short examples with python code&quot;,<br /> agent_memory=&quot;previous section discussed structured memory&quot;<br />)<br /><br />response = llm.invoke(prompt)</pre><p><strong>pattern 9: tool-first context<br /></strong>sometimes the best context is no context at all.<br />instead of injecting thousands of tokens from a database, spreadsheet, or log file, let the model call a tool: sql, calculator, search, knowledge graph, api, or code execution environment.<br />only the result of the tool call needs to enter the prompt. this reduces token use and usually improves factual accuracy.</p><pre>from langchain_openai import chatopenai<br />from langchain_community.utilities import sqldatabase<br />from langchain.chains import create_sql_query_chain<br /><br /># connect to the database<br />db = sqldatabase.from_uri(&quot;sqlite:///company.db&quot;)<br /><br />llm = chatopenai(model=&quot;gpt-4.1&quot;)<br /><br /># create a tool that converts natural language to sql<br />sql_chain = create_sql_query_chain(llm, db)<br /><br /># user question<br />user_query = &quot;what were the top 5 selling products in q1 2025?&quot;<br /><br /># execute the sql query<br />sql_query = sql_chain.invoke({&quot;question&quot;: user_query})<br />result = db.run(sql_query)<br /><br /># only the query result is sent to the llm<br />response = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; question: {user_query} sql result: {result}<br />answer the question based only on the sql result. &quot;&quot;&quot;)</pre><p><strong>pattern 10: context isolation in multi-agent systems</strong></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*mmejqobtty3qa4v2zwgfdw.png" /></figure><p>a common mistake in multi-agent systems is giving every agent access to every piece of information. a better design separates context by responsibility: planner, researcher, coder, reviewer and final response generator.<br />this reduces distraction, lowers cost and creates clearer responsibility boundaries.</p><pre>from langchain_openai import chatopenai<br /><br />llm = chatopenai(model=&quot;gpt-4.1&quot;)<br /><br /># planner agent<br />plan = llm.invoke(&quot;&quot;&quot; task: write a blog on context engineering.<br /> create an outline only. &quot;&quot;&quot;).content<br /><br /># research agent<br />research = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; outline: {plan}<br /> find supporting references and key technical concepts. &quot;&quot;&quot;).content<br /><br /># writer agent<br />draft = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; outline: {plan} research notes: {research}<br />write the first draft. &quot;&quot;&quot;).content<br /><br /># reviewer agent<br />review = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; review the following draft for:<br /> - technical accuracy<br /> - grammar<br /> - readability<br />draft: {draft} &quot;&quot;&quot;).content<br /><br /># final response generator<br />final_article = llm.invoke(f&quot;&quot;&quot; original draft: {draft} <br />reviewer feedback: {review} produce the final polished article. &quot;&quot;&quot;)<br /></pre><h3><strong>choosing the right strategy</strong></h3><blockquote>no strategy is free each comes with a cost worth knowing before you commit to it.</blockquote><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/842/1*pxmeggkhmat0yldsmln8cq.jpeg" /></figure><p><strong>practical implementation checklist</strong></p><ul><li>define a context budget before building the prompt.</li><li>retrieve more candidates than you send to the model.</li><li>re-rank retrieved chunks before final prompt construction.</li><li>compress long evidence into query-specific summaries.</li><li>remove duplicated or overlapping chunks.</li><li>keep recent turns in full; summarize the rest.</li><li>store agent state as structured fields.</li><li>use tools instead of injecting raw databases or large files.</li><li>isolate context between agents in multi-agent workflows.</li><li>log which context was used so failures can be debugged.</li></ul><h4><strong>final thoughts</strong></h4><blockquote>as language models continue to expand their context windows, the temptation will always be to send more information. the best ai systems usually do the opposite. they retrieve less, compress more, organize information intelligently, and provide the model with only what is necessary to solve the current problem.</blockquote><blockquote>none of this comes free. every pattern in this piece trades one cost , latency, complexity or the risk of dropping something relevant and for another benefit: precision, efficiency, or scale. the real skill isn’t memorizing these patterns; it’s knowing which cost your system can least afford, and designing around that constraint.</blockquote><blockquote>context engineering is therefore not just a workaround for context limits. it is a core discipline for building efficient, reliable, and production-ready llm applications. the future of llm applications will not be shaped only by models with the largest context windows. it will be shaped by systems that know exactly how to use the context they already have.</blockquote><h3>further reading</h3><ul><li><strong>a survey of context engineering for large language models<br /></strong><a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334">https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13334</a></li><li><strong>anthropic: effective context engineering for ai agents</strong><br /> <a href="https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents">https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents</a></li><li><strong>langchain: context engineering for agents</strong><br /> <a href="https://www.langchain.com/blog/context-engineering-for-agents">https://www.langchain.com/blog/context-engineering-for-agents</a></li><li><strong>lost in the middle : how language models use long contexts</strong><br /> <a href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172">https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172</a></li></ul><img alt="" height="1" AI Community Building Pulso: What it Actually Takes to Put Agentic AI in a Solo Practice https://pub.towardsai.net/building-pulso-what-it-actually-takes-to-put-agentic-ai-in-a-solo-practice-ea90157867d0?source=rss----98111c9905da---4 <h4>What we learned turning real AI capability into something a one-person clinic can really <strong>use, and afford.</strong></h4><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/0*g building pulso: what it actually takes to put agentic ai in a solo practice <h4>what we learned turning real ai capability into something a one-person clinic can really <strong>use, and afford.</strong></h4><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/0*gfttfdppi4nkh77v" /><figcaption>photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@nci?utm_source=medium&amp;utm_medium=referral">national cancer institute</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com?utm_source=medium&amp;utm_medium=referral">unsplash</a></figcaption></figure><h3>why i’m writing this</h3><p>most of what gets written about “agentic ai” lives a long way from the people it’s supposed to help. we talk about autonomous agents, orchestration, rag, benchmarks. meanwhile the nutritionist, the psychologist, the dentist who runs their own practice is still copying appointments into a notebook, typing up records at midnight, and answering “do you take insurance?” for the thousandth time.</p><p>pulso started in that gap. this isn’t a pitch. it’s an honest log of the engineering and product problems we hit while turning real ai capability into something that fits the day, and the budget, of a health professional who works mostly alone. some of these challenges we chose. others chose us.</p><h3>1. infrastructure that grows with you: why we run on railway</h3><p>the first hard call in a new product is rarely a feature. it’s the foundation. where this runs, how it grows, and what it costs while there’s still no revenue to justify anything fancy.</p><p>we moved off a heavier, more “enterprise” setup and onto <strong>railway</strong>, and it was a deliberate choice. not because it’s the cheapest or the trendiest, but because it gives us three things that matter right now:</p><ol><li><strong>deploy by git, no ceremony.</strong> commit, push, the environment ships itself. no one-hour pipeline to validate a copy fix.</li><li><strong>environments that actually mirror each other.</strong> we keep staging and production as sibling environments, same backend service, same postgres, same redis. that lets us validate in staging before touching real data, which in healthcare isn't a luxury, it's the job.</li><li><strong>predictable, modular cost.</strong> fastapi backend, database, and cache in one place, with the freedom to pull any piece out when (and if) growth asks for it.</li></ol><p>the word that did the heavy lifting was <strong>modular</strong>. we designed the system in layers that can be separated without rewriting the product: the messaging layer (whatsapp through a bsp), the agent layer (the ai flows), the domain layer (journeys, records, scheduling), and the usage and billing layer. each one can scale, get swapped, or become its own service later without dragging the rest down.</p><p>the lesson we keep coming back to: in the validation stage, the best infrastructure isn’t the one that survives a million users. it’s the one that <strong>doesn’t get in the way of learning fast</strong>, and that you won’t have to throw away once the learning turns into traction.</p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*bb90qggavrpqk1ck17nkmw.png" /></figure><h3>2. we built from a real pilot, not from guesses</h3><p>this is probably the most important decision we made, and it isn’t technical.</p><p>the classic way to get product wrong is simple. you imagine a solution, bring it to the customer finished, and ask “would you want this?”. the answer is almost always “yes, love it”. and it’s almost always a polite lie. people don’t want to let you down, so they praise ideas they’ll never use. that bias has a name and a whole body of work behind it. it’s the spine of <em>the mom test</em> by rob fitzpatrick, and it echoes uri levine’s “fall in love with the problem, not the solution”. the practical rule is to stop asking whether people like your idea and start digging into the problem and what they actually do.</p><p>that’s exactly how we worked. instead of building a bundle of features and asking if people liked it, we started from a <strong>real pilot</strong>, ran it through <strong>several validation sessions</strong>, and listened to the problem before proposing anything. every feature came out of a concrete pain we watched happen, not a roadmap we invented in a room:</p><ul><li><strong>audio-to-record transcription.</strong> it showed up because dictating is natural for someone seeing patients all day, and typing isn’t. the professional talks the way they would in the room, and the system transcribes, structures, and organizes it.</li><li><strong>help searching the literature.</strong> an agent that helps find and summarize references, because staying current competes with a packed schedule.</li><li><strong>a scheduling assistant that supports the front desk.</strong> many of these practices already have a receptionist the patients know and trust, the person who gives the whole thing its human touch. we were never there to replace them. the assistant books, confirms, and reminds on its own, and it lets the receptionist handle the manual cases, like setting up recurring appointments, right inside the conversations tab. the patient gets a smoother experience and the practice gets time back.</li><li><strong>hybrid ai and human control.</strong> maybe the subtlest lesson of all. the professional has to be able to take over the conversation at any moment. the ai handles volume, the human steps in when it matters. without that, nobody trusts it enough to let it run.</li></ul><p>the difference is the method. we listened to the problem and brought the solution, instead of bringing a solution and asking if they’d like it. sounds like a detail. it’s the difference between building what sells and building what fills up the repo.</p><h3>3. the gap between frontier ai and what solo professionals actually have</h3><p>there’s an almost absurd distance right now between what agentic ai can already do and what an independent professional actually has in their hands day to day.</p><p>models hold a natural conversation, transcribe, summarize, structure, schedule, remind. and yet most small practices still run on a personal whatsapp, a spreadsheet, and memory. the technology exists. the access doesn’t. it’s packaged into expensive, complex tools built for big clinics and networks, with onboarding that assumes an it team the solo professional never had.</p><p>that’s the thesis behind pulso, and it’s what moved us from the start: use that gap. take real ai capability, the same kind that powers polished products today, and wrap it so a person working alone can use it on day one, in the channel they already live in (whatsapp), at a <strong>fair price</strong>.</p><p>it was never about having the newest model. it’s about removing the friction between that model and the person who’d gain the most from it. the innovation here is as much about distribution and packaging as it is about technology.</p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*weocfpsdjj3oprns6uh7dq.png" /></figure><h3>4. per-tenant unit economics: measure the cost of ai before you scale it</h3><p>this is the least glamorous challenge and the most decisive one for any product that ships ai. every message a model handles has a cost. every transcription has a cost. every agent that answers on its own is spending real money. if you don’t measure that <strong>per customer</strong>, you’re flying blind, and you find out the hard way when the bill arrives.</p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*sj8n_-rjp6jpalwfiq3ehg.png" /></figure><p>so per-tenant usage control wasn’t a late “nice to have”. it was foundation. we built a usage meter tied to the pricing model, and gave it a name the customer understands without thinking about tokens: <strong>pulsos</strong>.</p><p>the trick is turning a technical cost into a unit the customer can reason about. a pulso is that unit. instead of tokens, message fees, and model bills, the professional buys a quota of pulsos for the period (monthly, quarterly, or yearly), and every action draws it down by a weight that mirrors what it actually costs us:</p><ul><li>a reply inside the 24-hour conversation window costs <strong>0 pulsos</strong>. it’s the cheapest message for everyone, so we don’t charge for it.</li><li>a utility message, a confirmation or a reminder, costs <strong>1 pulso</strong>.</li><li>an outbound promotional message costs <strong>3 pulsos</strong>. it’s the most expensive one on every side, so it weighs the most.</li></ul><p>the professional sees this in plain language (“info” and “outreach”, never “utility” and “marketing”) and always knows how much of the pack is left. underneath, that exact same weight feeds our <strong>unit economics</strong>. we know the margin per plan, per customer, per type of use, and we can answer the question that kills ai startups: <em>does this customer make money?</em></p><p>the message weights aren’t the whole cost, though. the single most expensive thing we run is the <strong>conversation agent</strong>, the back-and-forth that figures out what the patient wants and carries a booking all the way to a confirmed slot. it’s multi-turn by nature, and even with the right model and aggressive prompt caching, those turns add up fast. that’s the point: the most valuable feature is also one of the priciest to operate, and you have to see that cost per customer before you scale it, not after.</p><p>so there’s a second layer of cost engineering in how we use the models themselves. we route each task to the right one. a fast, cached model (claude haiku) handles the day-to-day patient conversations and the basic tasks. a stronger one (claude sonnet) takes the heavier work where quality matters more than speed: generating care journeys, importing medical records, and powering the literature agent. there’s a fallback for when something breaks. the expensive model only shows up where it earns its keep.</p><p>the lesson: in an ai product, unit economics isn’t a finance spreadsheet, it’s an architecture decision. measure per tenant from day one and you can scale with confidence. skip it and you scale the losses.</p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*ub2jeykjblmfurmbgvhb8w.png" /></figure><h3>a few more challenges worth logging</h3><p>those four were the pillars. but some problems only surface once you put agentic ai in front of a real patient, on whatsapp, about health. these three earn a spot in the article.</p><h3>5. safety in a clinical setting: a human in the loop, for real</h3><p>when the channel is about health, and sometimes mental health, “the agent got it wrong” stops being a bug and becomes a risk. we had to build crisis-signal detection with an ai confirmation step before anything fires, specifically so we don’t trigger a crisis response on a false positive (someone filling in an “emergency contact” field at signup, for example). and there had to be an off switch: a flag that pulls that detection out of production in seconds if it ever starts doing more harm than good. safety in a health product is less about the happy path and more about <strong>failing carefully</strong>.</p><h3>6. taming whatsapp: the platform’s rules as an engineering constraint</h3><p>whatsapp is not a friendly api. there’s a 24-hour window for conversations, templates that need approval, automatic categorization by meta (which decides on its own whether your message is utility or marketing), and sending limits. we went with each professional bringing their own number, activated with help from our team, and built the whole template and rate-limit layer around rules we don’t control. a good chunk of pulso’s invisible engineering is exactly that: making a smooth experience fit inside a platform full of sharp edges.</p><h3>7. the demo as a product: earning trust before you touch someone’s schedule</h3><p>here’s something we learned about distribution. you can’t scale this with a signup link, and the reason is easy to underestimate. a professional’s schedule is their professional life. handing it over to an ai is not a casual yes. so we stopped chasing volume and put trust first. what actually works is high-touch: short, focused meetings with demos we’ve prepared in advance, backed by real test numbers, so the person feels the product working before a purchase is even on the table.</p><p>and selling ai with screenshots doesn’t work anyway. nobody believes it until they try it. so we turned the demo itself into a product. the lead gets a code, sends it to a number, and lives the experience in their own hands: books a slot, dictates a record by voice, watches the assistant answer questions on its own. the same number serves both the demo and the real flow, with smart routing between the two. building that was its own challenge, but it’s what makes the “oh, now i get it” land in minutes, and it’s what earns the right to touch the schedule later.</p><h3>what’s next</h3><p>the next challenges are already on the horizon, and they follow the same logic of catching a window while it’s open: digital signing of records and prescriptions with the brazilian icp-brasil standard, deeper calendar integration, and fitting into a regulatory landscape that’s opening up to digital in healthcare. each one is, again, the same exercise: take a capability that already exists and make it reachable for someone who works alone.</p><p>if there’s one line that sums up what we’ve learned building pulso, it’s this. the most advanced technology in the world only becomes value when it fits into a real person’s routine, at a price they’re willing to pay. the rest is engineering to close that distance.</p><img alt="" height="1" src="https://medium.com/_/stat?event=post.clientviewed&amp;referrersource=full_rss&amp;postid=ea90157867d0" width="1" /><hr /><p><a href="https://pub.towardsai.net/building-pulso-what-it-actually-takes-to-put-agentic-ai-in-a-solo-practice-ea90157867d0">building pulso: what it actually takes to put agentic ai in a solo practice</a> was originally published in <a href="https://pub.towardsai.net">towards ai</a> on medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.</p> [LLMs, AI Agents, RAG, Research, AI Coding, AI Search, Cloud AI, Hardware, Enterprise AI, Companies, Claude AI, Loop Engineering]
AI Community Can Your Computer Run Nvidia’s 550B Model? Not Even Close, and the Reason Is Fascinating https://pub.towardsai.net/can-your-computer-run-nvidias-550b-model-not-even-close-and-the-reason-is-fascinating-cf27e1b3d351?source=rss----98111c9905da---4 <p><em>Nvidia’s Nemotron 3 Ultra has 550 billion parameters, it’s free to download, and somewhere in the back of every developer’s mind is the question, could I run this thing myself? The short answer can your computer run nvidia’s 550b model? not even close, and the reason is fascinating <p><em>nvidia’s nemotron 3 ultra has 550 billion parameters, it’s free to download, and somewhere in the back of every developer’s mind is the question, could i run this thing myself? the short answer is no, not on anything you would call a personal computer, and the interesting part is why. the obvious wall is memory, but the real wall shows up when you try to shrink the model small enough to fit, because the technique that makes it smaller also makes it start to fall apart. here is the honest math on what it would take, how far quantization actually gets you, and the surprising reason the last few gigabytes are the ones you can’t have.</em></p><figure><img alt="" src="https://cdn-images-1.medium.com/max/1024/1*hgelbr6et88yqymfksvoca.jpeg" /></figure><p>nvidia did something unusual with nemotron 3 ultra. it released a genuinely frontier-scale model, 550 billion parameters built for reasoning and agents, as a free, open-weight download that anyone can grab off hugging face. and the moment a model like that goes public, the same daydream starts in thousands of heads at once, could i run this on my own machine, right here, no api bills, no rate limits, just me and a frontier model on my own hardware.</p><p>it’s a fun question to chase, and chasing it teaches you more about how these models actually work than almost anything else. so let’s actually do the math, honestly, on whether you can fit nvidia’s 550b model on your computer, how much you would have to shrink it to try, and the genuinely surprising reason the shrinking hits a wall well before your hardware does. the answer is a layer-by-layer story with a real twist at the end.</p><h3>first, what quantization actually is, in plain terms</h3><p>if you already know this, skip ahead. if not, here’s the whole idea in one paragraph.</p><p>a neural network is a giant pile of numbers called weights. when you train a model, those numbers are usually stored at high precision, 16 bits each in a format called bf16, which is like writing every number with lots of decimal places. quantization is the act of rewriting those numbers with fewer digits, 8 bits, 4 bits, or even fewer, so each one takes up less space. the tradeoff is obvious, fewer digits means less memory and faster math, but also less precision, because you’re rounding every number to a coarser grid. push it too far and the rounding errors pile up until the model’s answers degrade. the entire art is in how far you can round before the model notices.</p><p>the practical reason anyone cares is memory. at full bf16 precision, nemotron 3 ultra’s 550 billion parameters need about 1.1 terabytes of gpu memory just to hold the weights, which is roughly eight to ten of the highest-end data-center gpus. that’s a serious cluster. quantize the same weights to 4 bits and the requirement drops to about 275 gigabytes, a quarter of the size. that’s the difference between a small server rack and something a well-funded team can actually run. every bit you shave off is money and hardware saved, which is why the crushing game has real stakes beyond bragging rights.</p><h3>now put those numbers against your actual computer</h3><p>here is where the daydream meets the hardware, and it is worth being concrete, because this is the question you actually came for.</p><p>a high-end gaming gpu, the kind in an enthusiast’s desktop, has around 24 to 32 gigabytes of memory. the model at its shipped 4-bit size needs about 275. so a single top-tier consumer graphics card holds roughly a tenth of what you would need, and that is before counting the extra memory required for the context window and the running computation, which adds more on top. you are not close. you are off by a factor of ten or more.</p><p>what about the machines people reach for precisely because they have a lot of memory? a maxed-out apple desktop with unified memory now ships in configurations up to several hundred gigabytes, and this is the one case where the raw number starts to look tantalizingly close to that 275-gigabyte figure. in principle, a top-spec unified-memory machine could hold a 4-bit version of the weights. but holding the weights is not the same as running the model well. on that kind of hardware you would be running inference on unified memory and cpu-class throughput rather than on the parallel tensor cores the model was built for, which means the model would technically load and then generate text at a speed measured in a trickle of tokens, not a usable stream. it’s the difference between owning a race car and owning the parts of a race car in your garage. technically present, not exactly drivable.</p><p>so the honest first verdict is simple. on a normal personal computer, a laptop or a single-gpu desktop, you cannot run nvidia’s 550b model, quantized or not. on an unusually memory-heavy workstation you can perhaps load a crushed version and watch it crawl. and that naturally leads to the obvious follow-up, if memory is the wall, why not just crush the model harder until it fits comfortably? that’s where the real story starts, and where it gets genuinely surprising.</p><h3>the twist, this model is already quantized at birth</h3><p>here’s where nemotron 3 ultra breaks the usual pattern. most models are trained in high precision and quantized afterward, which is a bit like writing a document in full detail and then photocopying it at lower and lower quality. nemotron 3 ultra was instead trained using what nvidia calls an nvfp4 recipe, a 4-bit floating-point format, from the start. the model learned its weights while already living in a 4-bit world, so it adapted to the coarse grid during training rather than being forced onto it afterward.</p><p>this matters enormously for our question. quantization-aware training produces a model that holds up far better at low precision than one crushed after the fact, because the model had a chance to compensate for the rounding while it was still learning. in effect, nvidia already did the hard part of the crushing for us, and did it the good way. the primary shipped checkpoint is the 4-bit one, not the full-precision one. the full bf16 version exists mostly as a reference for fine-tuning and for checking how much quality the quantization costs, not as the thing you’re meant to run.</p><p>so when someone asks “how far can we quantize the 550b model,” the honest first answer is, nvidia already took it to 4-bit and that’s the recommended production format. the interesting question is whether you can go below 4-bit, and that’s where it gets genuinely tricky.</p><h3>the critical insight, not all layers quantize equally</h3><p>here’s the thing most quick takes miss, and it’s the key to the whole puzzle. a large language model isn’t a uniform block of weights that you can crush evenly. different parts of the model do different jobs, and they tolerate rounding very differently.</p><p>nvidia’s own design makes this concrete. even in the 4-bit nemotron, nvidia deliberately kept several types of layers at higher precision, in bf16 or a format called mxfp8, rather than pushing them to 4-bit. specifically, the latent projection layers, the multi-token prediction layers, the query-key-value attention projections, and the embeddings were all held back from full quantization. the people who built the model, who understand it better than anyone, chose not to crush these particular layers, because doing so hurt stability.</p><p>that tells you something important. if the model’s own creators found that certain layers must stay at higher precision even at the 4-bit stage, those same layers are the ones that will resist any further crushing hardest. the attention projections, which decide what the model pays attention to, and the embeddings, which encode the meaning of every token, are precision-sensitive in a way the bulk of the network isn’t. there’s no free lunch where you uniformly drop everything to 2-bit and keep the quality. the moment you touch the sensitive layers, things break.</p><p>this is why serious quantization is never a single number. it’s a mixed-precision recipe, keep the fragile layers at higher precision, crush the tolerant layers hard, and spend your bit budget where it does the least damage. the question “how far can you quantize it” is really “which layers can you quantize how far,” and the answer differs for every layer in the network.</p><h3>the mixture-of-experts angle, where the bits actually are</h3><p>nemotron 3 ultra has another architectural feature that changes the math, and it cuts in an interesting direction. it is a mixture-of-experts model, which means that of its 550 billion total parameters, only about 55 billion are active on any given token. the model is made of many “expert” sub-networks, and a router picks a small subset to handle each token.</p><p>for memory, this is bad news for the crushing game in one sense, because you still have to hold all 550 billion parameters in memory even though only a tenth of them fire at once. every expert has to be resident so the router can reach it. you pay the storage bill for the whole model, not just the active part. so the moe structure is exactly why the model is so heavy to hold despite being relatively cheap to run.</p><p>but it’s good news in another sense, because the vast bulk of those 550 billion parameters live inside the experts, and the experts are the feed-forward layers that tend to be the most tolerant of aggressive quantization. the precision-sensitive machinery, the attention, the routing, the embeddings, is a relatively small fraction of the total parameter count. so the enormous expert bulk is exactly the part you can crush hardest, and it’s also the part that dominates your memory bill. that’s a fortunate alignment, the biggest, heaviest part of the model is also the most crushable, and the fragile part is small. this is why 4-bit works so well on this model in the first place, most of the weight is in crushable experts.</p><h3>so how far can you actually go, honestly</h3><p>put the pieces together and here’s the real answer, in tiers.</p><p>four-bit is the shipped, supported reality, and it already gives you the 4x memory reduction from full precision. nvidia trained the model to live there, so quality at 4-bit is close to the full-precision reference. if your question is “can i run this at 4-bit without much loss,” the answer is yes, that’s the intended state.</p><p>going to roughly 3-bit on the expert weights specifically, while keeping the sensitive layers at 4-bit or higher, is the frontier where community quantization work tends to operate. because the experts are tolerant and they dominate the parameter count, a well-designed mixed recipe that pushes the experts toward 3-bit and protects attention, embeddings, and routing can claw out meaningful additional memory savings while keeping the model mostly coherent. this is where the real craft lives, and it’s genuinely possible to do well.</p><p>below 3-bit, into 2-bit and lower, is where the model stops being itself, and the reason is the most interesting part of the whole story.</p><h3>the real villain, reasoning models break differently</h3><p>here’s the punchline that the memory math alone never tells you. nemotron 3 ultra is a reasoning model. it answers hard questions by first generating a long chain of intermediate reasoning steps and then producing a final answer. that design is exactly what makes it fragile to aggressive quantization, in a way a simple chatbot isn’t.</p><p>when you quantize aggressively, you introduce small errors into the model’s outputs, tiny mistakes in word choice, slightly wrong probabilities, occasional slips. in a single-shot task, like a one-line factual question, a small error is often harmless, the answer is still roughly right. but in a reasoning model, the output of each step becomes the input to the next step. a small error early in a chain of reasoning doesn’t stay small. it feeds forward, the next step reasons on top of the mistake, and by the time the model reaches its conclusion twenty steps later, the initial rounding error has compounded into a confidently wrong answer.</p><p>this is why practitioners specifically warn against low-bit quantization for reasoning workloads, even when the same quantization would be fine for casual chat. the damage doesn’t show up cleanly in the kind of single-answer benchmark that quick quantization tests use. it shows up as a slow rot in multi-step tasks, the model still sounds fluent, still forms grammatical sentences, but its long reasoning chains quietly derail more often. you can crush a chatbot and get a slightly dumber chatbot. crush a reasoning model too hard and you get something that sounds just as confident while being wrong in ways that are harder to catch.</p><p>that’s the real ceiling. it’s not the memory. it’s that the last few bits you’d love to remove are exactly the bits that keep long reasoning chains from falling apart, and this model’s entire value is in those chains. the floor on quantization here is set by error propagation, not by gigabytes.</p><h3>the honest takeaway</h3><p>so, can you run nvidia’s 550b model on your own computer. the satisfying answer is a set of nested truths. on normal personal hardware, no, the 4-bit model needs about 275 gigabytes of memory, more than ten times what a high-end consumer gpu holds, and on an unusually memory-rich workstation you can perhaps load it and watch it crawl. to fit it comfortably on hardware you own, you would have to crush it further than 4-bit, and that is exactly where it breaks. it already ships at 4-bit, so the first 4x of shrinking is done for you and done well. you can push the expert layers a bit further, toward 3-bit, if you protect the sensitive attention, embedding, and routing layers, because the experts are both the bulk and the most tolerant part. and you can’t go much below that without breaking the thing that makes the model worth running, its ability to hold a long chain of reasoning together, because quantization errors compound across reasoning steps in a way that single-shot tests hide. the model you could shrink small enough to fit is no longer the model you wanted to run.</p><p>the deeper lesson is one that applies to every big model, not just this one. quantization is not a volume knob you turn down until the sound gets bad. it’s a scalpel, and the skill is knowing which layers to cut deep and which to leave alone. the models that survive aggressive crushing are the ones where someone understood the anatomy. nemotron 3 ultra, already born at 4-bit with its fragile layers deliberately protected, is a model that tells you exactly where its own limits are if you read the design carefully. the bits it refuses to give up are the bits that matter most.</p><p><em>if you have pushed nemotron 3 ultra or another reasoning model to aggressive low-bit quantization, drop a comment with what you saw, especially on long multi-step tasks rather than single prompts. the place these models break is exactly the place quick benchmarks miss, and real accounts are worth more than any theoretical estimate.</em></p><img alt="" height="1" src="https://medium.com/_/stat?event=post.clientviewed&amp;referrersource=full_rss&amp;postid=cf27e1b3d351" width="1" /><hr /><p><a href="https://pub.towardsai.net/can-your-computer-run-nvidias-550b-model-not-even-close-and-the-reason-is-fascinating-cf27e1b3d351">can your computer run nvidia’s 550b model? not even close, and the reason is fascinating</a> was originally published in <a href="https://pub.towardsai.net">towards ai</a> on medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.</p> [LLMs, AI Agents, RAG, Research, AI Coding, Hardware, AI Tools, Companies, Loop Engineering]
